kurals.tamil:
அறிவற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி செறுவார்க்கும்
உள்ளழிக்க லாகா அரண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivatrang kaakkum karuvi seruvaarkkum
Ullazhikka laakaa aran.
kurals.meaning: Wisdom is a weapon that guards a person against ruin; it is also an inner fortress that even enemies cannot breach or destroy.
kurals.elementary: Imagine having a shield and a castle that nobody can ever take away from you. Valluvar says good sense is exactly that. It protects you from making ruinous mistakes, and no enemy can break into it, because it lives inside you.
kurals.university: The couplet sets up the governing metaphor of the chapter: arivu is both karuvi (an instrument or weapon) and aran (a fortress). The word அற்றம் (atram) means destruction, ruin, or a vulnerable moment of exposure. Parimelazhagan reads arivu as the faculty that keeps a person from falling into ruin. The second line moves the fortress inward: உள் (ul) is 'inside', so this is a stronghold that attackers (செறுவார், 'those who hate') cannot tear down from within. Placing the chapter in Porutpal is significant. For a king, forts, armies, and treasuries are external defences that can be besieged or bribed away, while discernment cannot be captured. The pairing of 'weapon' and 'wall' covers both active and passive defence. Stoic thought makes the same move with Marcus Aurelius's 'inner citadel', and the Dhammapada's image of the mind fortified like a city is similar.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In this endeavor there is no loss or diminution, and a little advancement on this path can protect one from the most dangerous type of fear.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna has just introduced buddhi-yoga, the discipline of understanding (2.39). He says that even a little of it acts as a protection against the greatest fear.
hinduism.tie_back: In both texts, discernment protects a person from ruin. The Gita stresses that even a small amount protects, while the Kural stresses that no enemy can destroy it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Protection-by-understanding matches well. The Gita's context is spiritual liberation from fear, not the Kural's worldly and political ruin. The fortress image is absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that when they are hauled before hostile rulers, they will be given wisdom that none of their opponents can overcome.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts present wisdom as a defence that adversaries cannot break down. This matches the Kural's second line closely.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on wisdom that enemies cannot overcome. In Luke the wisdom is divinely given for the moment, whereas the Kural means a cultivated personal faculty.

islam.quote_or_event: Joseph (Yusuf) interprets the king's dream of seven fat and seven lean cows. He counsels storing grain during the seven years of plenty so that Egypt survives the seven years of famine.
islam.explanation: Joseph's knowledge and foresight become Egypt's defence. His understanding protects the whole land from a disaster that armies and wealth could not have stopped.
islam.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural's claim that wisdom is a tool that guards against ruin. Here the ruin was a famine rather than an enemy.
islam._accuracy_note: Narrative illustration, not a direct statement. The 'protection from ruin' half matches; the 'fortress enemies cannot breach' half is only implied.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ecclesiastes describes a small city besieged by a great king. A poor wise man in it delivered the city by his wisdom, and the Preacher concludes that wisdom is better than strength and better than weapons of war.
judaism.explanation: Kohelet describes a town that walls and soldiers could not save, but one person's wisdom could. Ecclesiastes 7:19 adds that wisdom makes the wise stronger than ten rulers in a city.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts treat wisdom as the true defence of a besieged place, stronger than physical fortification.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in theme: wisdom as the real city-defence, better than weapons. Paraphrased rather than quoted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Realizing that this body is as fragile as a clay pot, and fortifying this mind like a well-fortified city, fight out Mara with the sword of wisdom.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells practitioners to treat the mind as a walled city and wisdom as the weapon used from inside it against Mara, the tempter.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's double image: wisdom as weapon (karuvi) and the mind as an unbreachable fortress (aran).
buddhism._accuracy_note: Remarkably close: both texts pair a fortress with a weapon, and both locate them in the mind and wisdom.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Trapped in the Cyclops Polyphemus's cave, Odysseus survives by cunning (metis) rather than force. He tells the giant his name is 'Nobody', blinds him, and escapes clinging beneath the sheep.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus has no strength to match a Cyclops. His mind is the only weapon and defence he has, and it saves him and his men.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Practical intelligence works here as the weapon that guards against ruin, as the Kural describes.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates wisdom as a weapon against destruction. Odysseus's metis is craftier and more trickster-like than Valluvar's ethical arivu, and the 'inner fortress' image is missing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure to which he can fly for refuge.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that the ruling faculty of reason, kept clear, is an inner stronghold that outside events and enemies cannot capture.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's 'inner fortress' (ul aran) almost word for word: reason as a citadel that attackers cannot overthrow.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close image (inner citadel). The Stoic emphasis is on freedom from passion, while the Kural emphasises discernment. Quote abridged from the Long translation.

kurals.tamil:
சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா தீதொரீஇ
நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்ப தறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Sendra idaththaal selavidaa theethoreei
Nandrinpaal uyppa tharivu.
kurals.meaning: Wisdom is not letting the mind run wherever it wanders. It holds the mind back from evil and steers it toward the good.
kurals.elementary: Your mind is a bit like a puppy that wants to run off in every direction. Wisdom is the leash. It stops the puppy from running into trouble and gently pulls it toward good things.
kurals.university: Here arivu is defined by its function over the mind (implied as the subject). சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா means 'not letting it go wherever it goes'. தீது ஒரீஇ means 'removing it from evil', and நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது means 'leading it toward the good'. Three movements are involved: restraint, withdrawal, and redirection. Wisdom is therefore not only knowing the good but actively governing attention and desire. Parimelazhagan glosses the object as the mind driven by the five senses. The image matches Indian and Greek charioteer models of the psyche (Katha Upanishad, Plato's Phaedrus), where intelligence holds the reins of the senses. The Buddhist 'fletcher straightening the arrow' image is similar. The Kural is notably positive: wisdom does not simply suppress the mind, it 'leads' it (uyppathu) somewhere better.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad teaches that the good (shreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person. The wise examine and distinguish them and choose the good; the fool chooses the pleasant. It then compares the body to a chariot, the senses to horses, and buddhi (discernment) to the charioteer holding the reins of the mind.
hinduism.explanation: Yama tells Nachiketas that discernment must choose between competing pulls and must rein in senses that would otherwise run wild, like untamed horses.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts describe wisdom as the faculty that stops the mind from going wherever it pulls and steers it to the good.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close structure: restrain the wandering senses and mind, and choose the good over the merely pleasant. Paraphrased because translations vary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul sums up the Christian moral life as turning away from evil and holding fast to good.
christianity.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's two moves: theethu oreei (removing oneself from evil) and nandrinpaal uyppathu (leading toward the good).
christianity._accuracy_note: Same two-part movement away from evil and toward good. Paul does not name the wandering mind or present this as the definition of wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises the person who holds the nafs (lower self) back from following its desires.
islam.tie_back: Both texts stress restraining the self from going wherever its inclinations lead.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on restraining inclination. The Qur'an grounds this in fear of God, not in 'wisdom' as such.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, 'Who is mighty?' and answers, 'One who subdues his (evil) inclination (yetzer).'
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah redefines strength as mastery over one's own impulses rather than power over others.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts see the key human capacity as governing the inner drive that pulls toward wrong.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close in substance (mastering impulse), but Avot calls this 'might' rather than 'wisdom'. Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a fletcher straightens an arrow shaft, even so the discerning man straightens his mind — so fickle and unsteady, so difficult to guard.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the discerning person to an arrow-maker who takes a crooked, wavering shaft and makes it straight.
buddhism.tie_back: In both texts the discerning faculty takes a restless, wandering mind and directs it true.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near match: a wise person governing a fickle mind. The 'away from evil, toward good' direction is implicit.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At a crossroads the young Heracles meets two women, Vice and Virtue. Vice offers an easy road of pleasure; Virtue offers a harder road of toil and honour. Heracles chooses Virtue.
greek_mythology.explanation: Prodicus's fable presents the moment of choice when desire pulls toward the easy path and judgment must turn it toward the good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural's turning of the mind away from evil and toward good.
greek_mythology.source: Prodicus, 'The Choice of Heracles', as retold in Xenophon, Memorabilia 2.1.21-34
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration of choosing the good over the pleasant. It is a single decisive choice rather than the ongoing steering of the mind the Kural describes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato's Socrates likens the soul to a charioteer driving two winged horses: one noble and obedient, the other unruly and pulled by appetite. The charioteer (reason) must rein in the unruly horse and guide the pair upward.
philosophy.explanation: Reason's job is to stop appetite from dragging the soul wherever it wants and to direct it toward the good.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural: arivu is the charioteer that keeps the mind from bolting and leads it toward the good.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Structural parallel is strong. Plato's tripartite soul is more elaborate than Valluvar's simple mind/wisdom pairing.

kurals.tamil:
எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Epporul yaaryaarvaaik ketpinum apporul
Meipporul kaanpa tharivu.
kurals.meaning: Whatever you hear, and from whomever you hear it, wisdom is seeing the real truth of that matter.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes people believe something just because a famous or important person said it. Sometimes they ignore something true because someone they don't like said it. Valluvar says a wise person looks at what was said and asks, 'Is this actually true?', no matter who said it.
kurals.university: This is among the most frequently quoted Kurals, often cited as an early statement of critical thinking. The repetition யார்யார் ('whoever, whoever') stresses that the speaker's status, reputation, or hostility is irrelevant. The contrast between பொருள் (porul, the thing said or its surface content) and மெய்ப்பொருள் (meipporul, its true substance) separates what is asserted from what is real. Two errors are ruled out. One is deference to authority, accepting a claim because of who said it. The other is the ad hominem, rejecting it for the same reason. The Kural is less radical than modern empiricism, because it assumes the truth can be discerned through judgment. Still, its location of arivu in the evaluation of claims, not in the collecting of them, anticipates the Buddhist Kalama Sutta and Aristotle's 'truth above friends'. For a king in Porutpal, this is also advice about handling the reports of ministers, spies, and flatterers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Rig Veda prays, 'Let noble thoughts come to us from every side' (ā no bhadrāḥ kratavo yantu viśvataḥ).
hinduism.explanation: This Vedic invocation is widely cited in India as a charter for openness: good insight is welcome whatever its source.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shares the Vedic openness to wisdom from any quarter, and adds the requirement that it be tested for real truth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the 'from anyone' half but not the critical 'discern the true substance' half. The popular rendering differs from literal translations (e.g. Griffith), so it is paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Thessalonians not to reject teachings outright or accept them uncritically, but to test everything and keep what holds true.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same method as the Kural: examine whatever you hear and hold onto its true substance.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close in method (test everything). It does not make the 'regardless of who speaks' point explicit.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an praises those who hear what is said, weigh it, and follow the best of it, and calls them ulu al-albab, 'people of understanding'.
islam.tie_back: Both texts define understanding as sifting what one hears to find what is truly best.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on listening critically and following the best. The source-independence point is implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, 'Who is wise?' and answers, 'One who learns from every person.'
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah defines the wise person as someone willing to receive truth from anyone, whatever their standing.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost a direct echo of the Kural's 'from whomever you hear it'.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near match on source-independence of wisdom. Avot emphasises humility in learning; the Kural emphasises critical discernment. Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells the Kalamas not to accept teachings merely because of report, tradition, scripture, logic, or the speaker's seeming competence, or because 'this contemplative is our teacher'. They should accept a teaching only when they know for themselves that it is skillful and leads to welfare.
buddhism.explanation: The Kalama Sutta is the classic Buddhist charter for evaluating claims on their merits rather than on the authority of the speaker.
buddhism.tie_back: It makes the same point as the Kural: a claim's truth is not settled by who says it; wisdom sees its real substance.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel on independence from speaker authority. Paraphrased from the Thanissaro translation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, cursed by Apollo so that no one would believe her, foretells the fall of Troy and Agamemnon's murder. Her hearers dismiss her true words because of who she is.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Trojans and the Argive chorus judge the prophecies by the speaker (a 'mad' captive) and not by their content, and ruin follows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the failure the Kural warns against: failing to see the truth of a claim because of the person saying it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A negative example rather than a direct teaching. In the myth the disbelief is imposed by a divine curse, not by the listeners' own failure of judgment alone.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For, while both are dear, piety requires us to honour truth above our friends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle criticises the Platonic Form of the Good even though Plato was his teacher and friend. He insists that truth outranks loyalty to any person.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts put the truth of a claim above the identity or status of the person who holds it.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.6, 1096a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on truth over persons. Aristotle's context is a philosophical disagreement with a revered teacher, which narrows the Kural's general principle.

kurals.tamil:
எண்பொருள வாகச் செலச்சொல்லித் தான்பிறர்வாய்
நுண்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Enporula vaagach selachcholli thaanpirarvaai
Nunporul kaanpa tharivu.
kurals.meaning: Wisdom is speaking so that your meaning is easily grasped and sinks into the listener's mind, and also perceiving the subtle meaning in what others say.
kurals.elementary: A wise person does two things with words. When they talk, they explain things so clearly that others understand easily. When they listen, they catch even the small, hidden points in what others are saying.
kurals.university: The couplet describes wisdom in communication as running in two directions. In speaking, எண்பொருள ஆக means 'so that the meaning is easy' and செலச் சொல்லி means 'speaking so that it goes in', that is, lodges in the listener. In listening, நுண்பொருள் காண்பது means 'seeing the subtle or fine meaning' in another's words. The contrast between எண் (easy, simple) and நுண் (subtle, fine) is deliberate. The wise person simplifies when giving and refines when receiving. This is a sophisticated account of communicative intelligence, close to what classical rhetoric called knowing one's audience (Plato's Phaedrus) and to hermeneutic charity in interpreting others. For rulers and ministers, the Porutpal setting, it is practical advice: make your orders clear, and read the unstated intentions of envoys and courtiers.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes disciplined speech as speech shaped for its effect on the listener: true, agreeable, and helpful.
hinduism.tie_back: This covers the speaking half of the Kural, speaking so that words land well with the hearer.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Partial match. It addresses the ethics of pleasing, beneficial speech but not clarity of explanation, and it omits the listening half entirely.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges speech adapted to each listener: gracious, apt, and responsive to the person being answered.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts see wise speech as speech tailored to land with the hearer. Knowing 'how to answer every man' requires grasping what each person means.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good on speaking aptly to each listener. The subtle-listening half is only implied.

islam.quote_or_event: “Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a way that is best.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an ties hikmah (wisdom) directly to how one speaks: persuasively, kindly, and in the best manner for the audience.
islam.tie_back: Both texts connect wisdom with speaking in a way that actually reaches the hearer.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the effective-speech half and explicitly names wisdom. The subtle-listening half is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah lists seven marks of a wise person: he does not speak before one greater in wisdom, does not interrupt, is not hasty to answer, asks relevant questions and answers to the point, speaks on first things first, admits when he has not understood, and acknowledges the truth.
judaism.explanation: The sage is defined by disciplined conversation: careful listening, fitting replies, and orderly speech.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Avot treats wisdom as skill in both hearing and speaking.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good two-way match covering both listening and speaking. Avot emphasises etiquette and order more than the Kural's clarity and subtle perception. Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “That monk who has control over his tongue, is moderate in speech, unassuming and who explains the Teaching in both letter and spirit — whatever he says is pleasing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises the monk whose speech conveys both the letter and the inner meaning of the Dhamma, and so is received well.
buddhism.tie_back: Explaining 'in letter and spirit' parallels the Kural's pairing of plain meaning with subtle meaning, and speech that 'pleases' reaches the hearer.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the effective-explanation half. It lacks the explicit instruction to perceive subtle meaning in others' words.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Nestor of Pylos is introduced as the clear-voiced orator 'from whose tongue flowed speech sweeter than honey'. He is repeatedly sent to reconcile quarrelling chiefs because his words reach them.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor is Homer's model of the counsellor whose speech persuades because it is well judged for his audience.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He exemplifies the speaking half of the Kural: words that go in and settle in the hearer's mind.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates persuasive, audience-fit speech but not subtle listening. Nestor's advice is also sometimes ignored.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that a true art of speech requires knowing the nature of the soul. The speaker must identify what kind of soul he addresses and fit the speech to it, simple speech to a simple soul and complex speech to a complex one.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, real rhetoric depends on understanding the listener, which in turn requires a subtle perception of other minds.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts see communicative wisdom as fitting speech to the hearer and perceiving what lies within others.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual parallel covering both audience-fit speech and insight into others. Plato is theorising an art of rhetoric, while the Kural gives a trait of character.

kurals.tamil:
உலகம் தழீஇய தொட்பம் மலர்தலும்
கூம்பலும் இல்ல தறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulagam thazheeiya thotpam malarthalum
Koombalum illa tharivu.
kurals.meaning: Excellence lies in befriending the worthy of the world. Wisdom lies in keeping that friendship steady, without first blossoming out and then closing up.
kurals.elementary: Some people are super friendly one day and cold the next, like a flower that opens in the morning and shuts at night. Valluvar says it is smart to make friends with good people. It is wise to stay the same kind friend every day, not hot one day and cold the next.
kurals.university: This is the most debated couplet in the chapter. ஒட்பம் (otpam) means excellence or sagacity, and உலகம் (ulagam, 'the world') is read by Parimelazhagan and most commentators as 'the great ones of the world' (uyarndhor). The first half therefore says that true excellence is to befriend the eminent. The second half uses a flower image: மலர்தல் (blooming, opening) and கூம்பல் (closing, as a flower does at dusk). Wisdom is keeping that friendship constant, neither over-effusive at the start nor withdrawing later. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi, Mu. Varadarasan) take the flower image more broadly as emotional equanimity in joy and sorrow. Both readings stress stability: arivu produces steadiness of disposition, especially in relationships. Aristotle's view that friendships of the good endure because goodness endures is a close parallel.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not disturbed in mind even amidst the threefold miseries or elated when there is happiness, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna describes the sthita-prajna, the person of steady wisdom, who neither swells in good times nor collapses in bad.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's 'no blooming and no closing', which the equanimity reading takes as the mark of wisdom.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match to the equanimity reading. It misses the traditional commentary's specific focus on constancy in friendship with the great.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs defines true friendship by its constancy, the same in good times and in hardship.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's steady friendship, neither opening wide nor shutting, is the friend who 'loveth at all times'.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match to the friendship-constancy reading. It does not link this to 'wisdom' or to choosing eminent friends.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches believers to hold an even keel: not crushed by loss, not puffed up by gain.
islam.tie_back: This parallels the flower image of neither blooming (exulting) nor closing (despairing).
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the equanimity reading well but not the friendship reading.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah teaches that any love dependent on some particular thing ceases when that thing ceases, while love not dependent on anything never ceases. The love of David and Jonathan is its example.
judaism.explanation: Avot distinguishes fickle, conditional attachment from steady love that does not wax and wane with circumstances.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's steady friendship, which does not open and close with changing fortunes.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match to the constancy-in-friendship reading. Paraphrased; numbering varies between 5:16 and 5:19 in some editions.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sigalovada Sutta the Buddha describes the true-hearted friend as one who is the same in happiness and in sorrow. Such a friend does not desert you in trouble and would even give up his life for you.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists the marks of genuine friendship to help a layman tell steady friends from fair-weather ones.
buddhism.tie_back: 'The same in happiness and sorrow' is the Kural's friend who neither blooms nor closes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close to the traditional friendship reading. Paraphrased from Narada Thera's translation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Pylades stays with Orestes through exile, madness, and mortal danger. In Iphigenia in Tauris, when only one of them may leave alive, each insists on dying for the other.
greek_mythology.explanation: Orestes and Pylades became the Greek byword for friendship that holds steady whatever the circumstances.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They embody the Kural's friendship that never closes up when fortune turns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates steadfast friendship. It is not framed as 'wisdom', and the 'befriending the great' element is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that friendships of utility and pleasure dissolve easily, but the friendship of the good lasts: “their friendship lasts as long as they are good — and goodness is an enduring thing.”
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle the best friendship is between good people and is stable because it rests on character, not on changing advantage or pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts link friendship with the excellent to a constancy that neither blooms nor fades.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.3, 1156b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close to the traditional reading (befriend the good; the friendship stays constant). Quote abridged from the Ross translation.

kurals.tamil:
எவ்வ துறைவது உலகம் உலகத்தோடு
அவ்வ துறைவ தறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Evva thuraivathu ulagam ulagaththodu
Avva thuraiva tharivu.
kurals.meaning: Wisdom is living in harmony with the world: conducting oneself as the world (the worthy) conducts itself.
kurals.elementary: Every place has its own ways of doing things. A wise person notices how good people around them behave and fits in with them, instead of being odd or rude just to stand out.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on the parallel எவ்வது / அவ்வது ('in whatever way / in that way') and on the verb உறைதல் (to dwell or abide). Wisdom is to abide with the world in the way the world abides. As in 425, Parimelazhagan takes ulagam to mean the uyarndhor, the worthy or great of the world, not the crowd. The Kural is therefore not a call to conformity with the majority but to conduct in step with the accepted norms of the good. It still carries a real social insight: discernment includes reading context and custom and not acting eccentrically. This complements 423. There, wisdom judges claims independently; here, wisdom adapts one's conduct to the settled ways of good society. Parallels range from the Talmudic 'never deviate from local custom' to Paul's 'all things to all men' and Descartes's provisional maxim of following his country's customs.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “So as not to disrupt the minds of ignorant men attached to the fruitive results of prescribed duties, a learned person should not induce them to stop work. Rather, by working in the spirit of devotion, he should engage them in all sorts of activities.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna advises the wise not to set themselves apart and unsettle ordinary people. They should act alongside them in the accepted way (compare 3.21: whatever the great do, others follow).
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts see wisdom as moving in step with the world instead of standing apart from it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in advising the wise to act in harmony with society. The Gita's aim is to avoid confusing the unenlightened, a more pedagogical motive than the Kural's.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes adapting his conduct to Jews, Gentiles, and the weak alike: living as they live, so as to reach them.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat adapting to the ways of those around you as wise and effective.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on adaptive conduct. Paul's goal is evangelistic, while the Kural's is general social wisdom.

islam.quote_or_event: Ali ibn Abi Talib said: speak to people according to what they understand. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?
islam.explanation: Bukhari records Ali's teaching in the Book of Knowledge: the wise adapt what they say to the capacity and ways of their audience.
islam.tie_back: Both texts see wisdom as fitting oneself to the people among whom one lives and speaks.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Knowledge, no. 127 (saying of Ali)
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the adaptive principle but is limited to speech. It is a Companion's saying, not a prophetic one. Paraphrased; translations vary.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that a person should never deviate from local custom. When Moses ascended on high he did not eat bread, and when the angels descended to visit Abraham they appeared to eat.
judaism.explanation: Even Moses and the angels adjusted their behaviour to the realm they were in, and the Talmud draws a general rule of wise conduct from this.
judaism.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural's point: live as the world you are in lives.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close parallel ('do not deviate from custom'). Paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says: 'I do not dispute with the world; the world disputes with me.' What the wise in the world agree does not exist, he too says does not exist; what they agree exists, he too says exists.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha presents himself as not contrary for its own sake. He aligns his statements with what the wise of the world accept.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural and Parimelazhagan's reading that one should abide as the wise of the world abide.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking match, including the 'wise of the world' nuance. It concerns agreement in statements rather than conduct generally. Paraphrased.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus is introduced as polytropos, 'the man of many turns', who 'saw the cities of many men and learned their mind'. He survives by adapting his manner to each people and court he encounters.
greek_mythology.explanation: His defining trait is adaptability: reading each new society and conducting himself accordingly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He illustrates the Kural's wisdom of moving with the world as the world moves.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Adaptability matches. Odysseus's flexibility is often strategic deception, which is more cunning than the Kural's harmonious conduct.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The first maxim of Descartes's provisional moral code is to obey the laws and customs of his country, and to govern himself by the most moderate opinions of the most sensible people he would live among.
philosophy.explanation: While doubting everything in theory, Descartes decides that in practice a wise person lives by the settled customs of sensible people around him.
philosophy.tie_back: This closely matches the Kural, including its implicit restriction to the sensible or worthy, as Parimelazhagan reads it.
philosophy.source: René Descartes, Discourse on the Method, Part 3
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close parallel: conform to the customs of the most sensible. Paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவுடையார் ஆவ தறிவார் அறிவிலார்
அஃதறி கல்லா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar aava tharivaar arivilaar
Aqdhari kallaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: The wise know beforehand what is going to happen; the unwise are those who cannot know it.
kurals.elementary: If you see dark clouds, you know rain is coming and take an umbrella. A wise person is good at spotting what is going to happen next, while a foolish person gets caught by surprise every time.
kurals.university: This couplet defines wisdom and its lack by one criterion: foresight. ஆவது அறிவார் means 'they know what will come to be'. The second line mirrors it: the unwise are precisely those who cannot know that (அஃது அறிகல்லாதவர்). Commentators take ஆவது to mean the outcome or consequence of present actions and circumstances, not supernatural prophecy. Arivu here is predictive practical judgment, the ability to read causes forward to their effects. The Talmudic definition 'who is wise? One who sees what will be born' is almost a translation. Aristotle's phronesis includes deliberating well about what conduces to the good in the long run, and Hesiod's Prometheus (forethought) and Epimetheus (afterthought) personify the Kural's opposition. The couplet also prepares for 429, where foresight becomes protection.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “That which in the beginning may be just like poison but at the end is just like nectar and which awakens one to self-realization is said to be happiness in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that sattvic understanding looks past immediate appearances to eventual outcomes, choosing what is bitter now but sweet in the end.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts define higher understanding by the ability to see how things will turn out.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Captures foresight of consequences indirectly. The Gita is classifying kinds of happiness, not directly defining wisdom as foresight.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus points to the ordinary prudence of thinking ahead to where a project will end before starting it. He contrasts this with the builder who is mocked for being unable to finish.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts define good sense as knowing in advance how things will turn out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on foresight of outcomes. It is used as an analogy for counting the cost of discipleship.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said: the wise (al-kayyis) is one who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death. The incapable (al-'ajiz) is one who follows his desires and merely hopes in Allah.
islam.explanation: The hadith defines intelligence by forward-looking action and folly by living only for the moment.
islam.tie_back: Both texts contrast the wise, who look ahead to what is coming, with the foolish, who cannot.
islam._accuracy_note: Close in contrasting forward-looking wisdom with folly. The foresight is eschatological, not worldly. The hadith's chain is graded hasan by Tirmidhi but weak by some scholars. Paraphrased.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud asks, 'Who is wise?' and answers, 'One who sees what will be born' (ha-ro'eh et ha-nolad), meaning one who foresees the outcome of things.
judaism.explanation: In Alexander the Great's dialogue with the elders of the Negev, the rabbis define wisdom as foresight of consequences.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost identical to the Kural: the wise know what will come to be.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim conceptual parallel. Paraphrased from the Hebrew; English renderings vary.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Future Dangers suttas the Buddha urges monks to consider dangers not yet arrived (old age, illness, famine, strife, corruption of the teaching) and to strive now, while conditions are favourable.
buddhism.explanation: The wise practitioner looks ahead to what is coming and acts before it arrives.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see knowing what is coming as the mark of wisdom.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on foresight. The sutta is a meditation practice, not a definition of wisdom. Paraphrased from the Thanissaro translation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Prometheus ('Forethought') warns his brother Epimetheus ('Afterthought') never to accept a gift from Zeus. Epimetheus accepts Pandora anyway and understands the harm only after it has come.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod builds the two brothers' names and fates on the contrast between foresight and hindsight.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This personifies the Kural exactly: the wise know what will come; the unwise know only too late.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near-perfect mythic embodiment of the Kural's foresight/folly opposition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “It is thought to be the mark of a man of practical wisdom to be able to deliberate well about what is good and expedient for himself... about what sorts of thing conduce to the good life in general.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines phronesis as sound deliberation about what leads to good ends, which requires foreseeing consequences.
philosophy.tie_back: Both texts see practical wisdom as seeing where actions lead.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 6.5, 1140a (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on practical wisdom generally. Foresight is implied in deliberation rather than named as the defining trait. Quote abridged.

kurals.tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தஞ்சாமை பேதைமை அஞ்சுவது
அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Anjuva thanjaamai pethaimai anjuvathu
Anjal arivaar thozhil.
kurals.meaning: Not fearing what ought to be feared is folly; fearing what ought to be feared is the way of the wise.
kurals.elementary: Being brave does not mean being scared of nothing. A person who isn't afraid of touching a hot stove or running across a busy road is not brave, just foolish. Wise people are careful about the things that really are dangerous.
kurals.university: The couplet rests on the repeated verb அஞ்சு (to fear) in a tight chiastic pattern. அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை ('not fearing the fearworthy') is பேதைமை (folly), and அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் ('fearing the fearworthy') is the practice (தொழில்) of the wise. Fear is treated not as a weakness to overcome but as an emotion to calibrate. Commentators apply it to wrongdoing, the anger of the powerful, and real dangers. This is almost exactly Aristotle's doctrine of courage as a mean: the brave person fears the right things in the right way, and fearlessness toward everything is rashness. The Dhammapada (317) and Proverbs (14:16) make the same point. In the Porutpal context, a king who fears nothing, not even enemies, public anger, or his own misdeeds, is a danger to the state.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, that understanding by which one knows what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, what is to be feared and what is not to be feared, what is binding and what is liberating, is in the mode of goodness.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines sattvic buddhi (clear understanding) partly as knowing what is and is not to be feared.
hinduism.tie_back: This is a direct parallel: both texts identify correctly sorting what is fearworthy as a function of true understanding.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact conceptual match, since both place knowing what to fear within buddhi/arivu.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus redirects his disciples' fear away from human persecutors and toward what is truly to be feared.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts teach that the issue is not whether to fear but what to fear.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match on calibrating fear. The object of right fear is divine judgment, whereas the Kural's is general.

islam.quote_or_event: “Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an connects knowledge ('ilm) directly with rightly placed fear (khashya) of God.
islam.tie_back: Both texts link knowledge with fearing what should be feared.
islam._accuracy_note: Close link between knowledge and right fear. The object is specifically God, not dangers in general.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A wise man feareth, and departeth from evil; but the fool behaveth overbearingly, and is confident.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the wise man, who is afraid of evil and avoids it, with the fool, who charges ahead full of confidence.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost a paraphrase of the Kural: the wise fear the fearworthy, and the fool fears nothing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-perfect match of the wise/fool contrast on fear.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Those who see something to fear where there is nothing to fear, and see nothing to fear where there is something to fear — upholding false views, they go to the state of woe.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha condemns misplaced fear in both directions, fearing the harmless and ignoring the truly dangerous, as wrong view.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's exact claim, extended to the opposite error as well.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Icarus ignores his father Daedalus's warning not to fly too near the sun. Exulting in flight and without fear, he soars upward until the wax of his wings melts and he falls into the sea.
greek_mythology.explanation: Icarus's lack of fear of a real danger, which his wiser father rightly feared, destroys him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural's first line: not fearing what should be feared is folly.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Clear narrative illustration of fearless folly. Daedalus embodies the wise fear only implicitly.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The man, then, who faces and who fears the right things and from the right motive, in the right way and at the right time, and who feels confidence under the corresponding conditions, is brave.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle defines courage not as fearlessness but as fearing the right things appropriately. Excess of confidence is rashness.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis stated as moral theory: fearing the fearworthy is wisdom, and not fearing it is folly.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 3.7, 1115b (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close parallel. Aristotle frames it as courage while Valluvar frames it as wisdom, but the calibration of fear is identical.

kurals.tamil:
எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க் கில்லை
அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ethirathaak kaakkum arivinaark killai
Athira varuvathor noi.
kurals.meaning: For the wise who guard in advance against what is coming, there is no calamity that strikes them so as to make them tremble.
kurals.elementary: If you know a storm is coming and you close the windows and bring in your toys, the storm can't really hurt you. Wise people prepare ahead of time, so when trouble comes it doesn't shake them.
kurals.university: Building on 427 (knowing what will come), this couplet adds action: எதிரதாக் காக்கும் means 'guarding against it as something ahead', that is, protecting oneself before a danger arrives. The result: இல்லை அதிர வருவதோர் நோய் ('there is no affliction that comes so as to make them shudder'). நோய் (noi) literally means disease but is used broadly for suffering or calamity, and அதிர (to shake or tremble) vividly describes the shock of being unprepared. The claim is not that the wise escape every misfortune but that nothing catches them off guard. This parallels the Stoic premeditatio malorum, the Panchatantra fable of the three fish, and Jesus's parable of the house built on rock. It links back to 421's image of arivu as a protective weapon.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Panchatantra, three fish in a pond overhear fishermen planning to return. Anagatavidhata ('Provider-for-the-future') leaves at once for another pond. Pratyutpannamati ('Ready-wit') escapes by playing dead. Yadbhavishya ('What-will-be-will-be') does nothing and is caught.
hinduism.explanation: The fable ranks prudence by foresight. The fish who guards against danger before it arrives survives with no distress at all.
hinduism.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural: the one who guards against what is coming is untouched by calamity.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative embodiment. The Panchatantra is a niti-shastra (practical wisdom) text, in the same genre as Porutpal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus contrasts the wise builder, who prepared a foundation before the storm, with the foolish builder whose house collapsed.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts teach that the wise prepare beforehand, so the storm does not bring them down.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on advance preparation making one unshakable. In the parable the 'foundation' is obedience to Jesus's words.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allah. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow — and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an calls believers to look ahead to 'tomorrow' (the Hereafter) and prepare for it now.
islam.tie_back: Both texts urge guarding in advance against what is coming.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the forward-looking preparation. The Qur'an's 'tomorrow' is primarily eschatological rather than worldly calamity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A prudent man seeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the thoughtless pass on, and are punished.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the prudent person, who sees trouble coming and takes cover, with the naive, who walk straight into it.
judaism.tie_back: This is nearly the same thought as the Kural: foresight plus precaution means calamity does not strike.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a border city is closely guarded both within and without, even so, guard yourself. Do not let slip this opportunity (for spiritual growth). For those who let slip this opportunity grieve when consigned to hell.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the image of a frontier city that guards itself before an attack comes. Those who fail to prepare later grieve.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts teach that guarding in advance prevents later suffering.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on advance guarding and its protection. The context is spiritual opportunity rather than worldly calamity.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Forewarned by Circe about the Sirens, Odysseus prepares before reaching them. He seals his crew's ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast, so the ship passes unharmed where others have perished.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus turns foreknowledge into precaution and faces a lethal danger without being destroyed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's claim: guard against what is ahead, and it will not strike you down.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close narrative match of foresight plus precaution.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges his friend Lucilius to anticipate every misfortune (exile, loss, disaster) in advance. Nothing should be unexpected, and what has been foreseen strikes more lightly.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic practice of premeditatio malorum rehearses possible calamities so that, when they come, they do not overwhelm.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural's 'no affliction comes to make them tremble': prepared minds are not shaken.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close. Seneca emphasises psychological preparation, the Kural both practical and mental. Paraphrased.

kurals.tamil:
அறிவுடையார் எல்லா முடையார் அறிவிலார்
என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar ellaa mudaiyaar arivilaar
Ennudaiya renum ilar.
kurals.meaning: Those who possess wisdom possess everything; those who lack wisdom possess nothing, whatever else they may have.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone with a huge pile of money but no sense. They would probably lose it all or use it badly. Someone with good sense can build up whatever they need. Valluvar says good sense is the one thing that counts as having everything.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with a sweeping summary built on the verb உடைமை (possession) that gives the chapter its title. அறிவுடையார் எல்லாம் உடையார் means 'the possessors of wisdom are possessors of all'. என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் means 'whatever they possess, they have nothing'. The point is that wisdom is the meta-possession that makes other possessions useful and secure. Without it, wealth, power, and allies are squandered or turned against their holder. It is striking that this appears in Porutpal, the book on wealth and statecraft: Valluvar ranks arivu above porul (wealth) itself. The Talmud's 'if you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack?' and Socrates's argument in the Euthydemus that wisdom is the only unconditional good are close parallels. Solomon's story, in which he chooses wisdom and receives everything else too, dramatises the same claim.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “In this world, there is nothing so sublime and pure as transcendental knowledge. Such knowledge is the mature fruit of all mysticism.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna declares that nothing in the world equals knowledge (jnana) in worth or purifying power.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts rank wisdom above every other possession.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the supremacy of knowledge. The Gita's jnana is spiritual knowledge, while the Kural's arivu is practical wisdom. The 'fool has nothing' half is absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: When Solomon asks God only for “an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad”, God grants it and adds: “I have also given thee that which thou hast not asked, both riches, and honour.”
christianity.explanation: Solomon chooses discernment over wealth, long life, or victory, and receives the rest as well.
christianity.tie_back: This dramatises the Kural: the one who has wisdom has everything.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match. In the story riches are added as a divine reward rather than flowing from wisdom itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will remember except those of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an calls hikmah (wisdom) a gift containing 'much good' (khayran kathiran).
islam.tie_back: Both texts treat wisdom as the possession that brings abundant good.
islam._accuracy_note: Close. The Qur'an says 'much good' rather than 'everything', and does not state the 'fool has nothing' converse.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud cites a popular saying: if one has acquired knowledge (da'at), what does he lack? If one lacks knowledge, what has he acquired?
judaism.explanation: The rabbis hold that knowledge is the possession that makes every other possession worthwhile, and without it nothing else counts.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural in both halves, with an almost identical structure.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-verbatim parallel of both halves. Paraphrased from the Aramaic; renderings vary.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better it is to live one day wise and meditative than to live a hundred years foolish and uncontrolled.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada holds that a single day of wisdom outweighs a century of foolish life.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see wisdom as making a life full and its absence as making everything else worthless.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Captures the supremacy of wisdom over quantity of life. It speaks of years rather than possessions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Zeus swallows Metis, the goddess of wisdom and counsel, so that her wisdom becomes his own. Only then is his rule secure, and Athena is later born from his head.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Hesiod, Zeus's supreme and lasting kingship depends on possessing wisdom within himself.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This mythically parallels the Kural: possessing wisdom secures possession of all.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Symbolic parallel: sovereignty secured by internalising wisdom. The myth is also about preventing a successor, so the match is partial.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues that wealth, health, beauty, and power are neither good nor bad in themselves. Guided by wisdom they become great goods, and guided by ignorance great evils. He concludes that wisdom is the only good and ignorance the only evil.
philosophy.explanation: In this dialogue with young Clinias, Socrates shows that all other possessions depend on wisdom for their value.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's logic exactly: with wisdom one has everything, and without it one has nothing, whatever one owns.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close philosophical parallel to both halves. Paraphrased from the Jowett translation.
